title: Bhagat Singh
hookLine: born into a Sikh family, the young revolutionary later wrote of doubting God, and is honored across Punjab

lines: THE SAME FACE ON TRUCKS AND WALLS.
A PRISON CELL, AND A PEN.
cards: On a truck's back panel, a college wall, a sticker on a scooter: the same young face, a mustache, sometimes a turban, sometimes a hat tilted to one side.
Ask the driver who it is and you'll get two words, said with real pride. Bhagat Singh. Ask what he believed about God, and the answer gets more interesting.
He was born into a Sikh family. And near the end of his short life, in a prison cell, he wrote out, as carefully as he could, why he no longer believed.

teach.b: Bhagat Singh grew up in a Sikh household in Punjab, in a family already caught up in the struggle against British rule.

teach.h: ARMED STRUGGLE, A TRIAL, THE GALLOWS.
teach.b: As a young man he turned to armed struggle, and that path ended in a trial in Lahore. He was hanged there with two companions, Sukhdev and Rajguru.

While waiting in prison he wrote a piece titled Why I Am an Atheist. He explains, plainly and without mockery, how he came to doubt God, and insists he got there by thinking it through, not out of pride.
He writes, too, that he expects to face the gallows without turning to belief for comfort at the end. He's honored across Punjab and beyond by religious and non-religious people alike.
Some Sikhs who pray every morning keep his picture on the wall; those who share his doubt claim him too. Nobody needs to settle his beliefs to honor his courage and his candor.
Guru Nanak gives the Sikh measure of a life at Ang 62 of the Guru Granth Sahib: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living.
Bhagat Singh's conclusions about God are his own, and Sikh teaching doesn't share them. What his admirers point to is that he didn't pretend. He said what he thought, and lived it to the end.

how: Bhagat Singh is remembered across Punjab, by Sikhs and by others, as a shaheed of the freedom struggle; his picture hangs in homes and shops, and his anniversary is marked with gatherings.

o: keep quiet and let people assume.

games.why: he wrote Why I Am an Atheist, explaining plainly, without mockery, how he came to doubt.

practice: Bring to mind someone who doesn't believe what you believe, or believes nothing at all, and who told you so honestly.

Notice any urge to argue and let it pass on the breath out, then find one thing to respect in them: their honesty, their care, the way they thought it through. If you pray, keep Waheguru on the breath while you hold that respect.
